title: Probing-First Preference Matrix and Control Plane Design
content:
Purpose
This working note captures a proposal for a probe-driven, preference-matrix approach to multi-region traffic steering and the corresponding control plane responsibilities. Goal is to reduce user-observed latency and availability impact when regions have asymmetric performance or transient failures, while keeping operational complexity manageable for Dedicated/Private customers and the Hosted control plane.

Scope and constraints
- Applies to inbound API traffic (edge → regional frontends → regional backends). Does not cover egress routing or internal service-to-service routing.
- Must interoperate with both Anycast fronting (customers using global Anycast IPs) and GeoDNS+short-ttl approaches.
- Support per-tenant regional preferences (customer pins) and global operator policies (latency SLOs, cost windows).
- Failover behavior must preserve data-residency constraints for Private deployments (no cross-region failover unless explicitly allowed).

High-level idea: probing-first preference matrix
- Maintain a lightweight matrix per region pair for each public route: score(region_from, region_to) = f(latency, success_rate, capacity_headroom, penalty).
- Scores are driven primarily by active probing from global vantage points + passive telemetry (client latencies, backend error rates). Active probes run from: Anycast POPs, global health-prober fleet, and representative customer regions (edge lambdas where applicable).
- At decision time the control plane computes a ranked list of preferred target regions for a given source (inferred from EDNS-client-subnet, POP, or BGP location). The ranked list includes weights and an optional TKO flag (temporary knockout).

Why probe-first?
- DNS-based heuristics (GeoDNS) with only coarse affinity leads to suboptimal choices during partial outages or network anomalies. A probe-first model catches asymmetric path degradation (e.g., cross-continental link flaps) faster than waiting for customer errors.
- Probing allows us to implement gradual failover (traffic shifting) instead of binary flip, reducing cache churn and downstream load spikes.

Probe types and frequency
- Fast active probes: simple TCP/HTTP health checks from each POP to each region, frequency 5s for critical routes, 30s for lower-traffic ones.
- Extended probes: measure 95th/99th percentile RTT and TLS handshake times, frequency 60s.
- Canary probes: when a region recovers, use increase-in-frequency windowed probes (10s) to validate before scaling weight back up.
- Passive telemetry: sample real requests (1–205% depending on volume) for latency and success rate; used to confirm or override active probe signals.

Score function (proposal)
- Normalize inputs to 0..100 then compute: score = w_lat*lat_component + w_sr*success_component + w_cap*capacity_component - penalty
- Suggested weights: w_lat=0.5, w_sr=0.3, w_cap=0.2. Penalty is a tunable operator-level damping factor (e.g., for maintenance windows or region-wide incidents).
- Regions with score < threshold_low (e.g., 20) are flagged TKO for 5 min; if score remains low after successive windows they are ejected from ranking until operator clears or score recovers.

Integration with routing frontends
- Anycast case: POP-level routing remains primary. When POP receives request, local POP consults control plane ranking for the inferred source-to-region mapping and chooses local handling policy:
  - Preferred local: if local region score is within latency window (e.g., +15ms) of best remote region and capacity healthy → serve locally.
  - Forward with preference: otherwise forward to region with top score via internal overlay (HTTP proxy/GRPC). Forwarding uses weighted routing to ramp traffic.
- GeoDNS case: authoritative DNS returns ordered or weighted answers (short TTL ~30s) based on control plane ranking. For clients that ignore order, use weighted probabilities and reserve a fallback TTL for hard ejection.
- For Dedicated/Private customers with fixed egress IPs, proxy the same preference list via control-plane-driven routing policies injected into the customer-facing edge cluster (no public DNS change).

Failover modes and policies
- Soft-shift (recommended default): move traffic gradually using weight ramps (10% steps every 30s) while monitoring error/latency signals. Abort and roll back if errors spike above threshold.
- Immediate failover: used only for catastrophic full region outage detected by high-confidence signals (e.g., region telemetry down, many upstream providers quoting outage). This is a last-resort operator-level switch.

Control plane design responsibilities
- Compute preference matrices using feed from probing service and passive metrics. Store short-lived ranking blobs (TTL 30s) per route + per-source-region key.
- Provide low-latency read API for frontends/POP routers with per-request cache and soft-staleness tolerance (read-through fallback to last-known-good when control-plane unreachable).
- Offer a single source of truth for operator overrides, customer pinning, and maintenance windows. Overrides are applied on top of probe-derived ranking (with explicit metadata explaining why).

Operational considerations and SLOs
- Probe coverage SLO: 99.9% of POP→region probe windows completed within configured interval.
- Decision freshness SLO: 95th percentile of control plane responses < 150ms for cached reads; < 500ms for cold reads.
- Rollback safety: automatic rollback on error-rate increase > 2x baseline within a 60s window while ramping traffic.
- Observability: time-series for probe-latency, score, weight-changes, ejections. Must include causal context (which probe caused change).

Edge cases and special handling
- Private deployments with no cross-region failover: enforce a hard policy that score changes cannot trigger cross-region routing unless customer flag enabled; show clear dashboard flagging suppressed ejections.
- GeoDNS staleness: clients with cached long TTLs can continue to hit degraded region; therefore combine DNS strategy with overlay routing where feasible (e.g., HTTP redirect or client-side SDK logic to respect X-Region-Preference header).

Testing plan and ramp strategy
- Unit tests for scoring logic with synthetic latency/failure traces.
- Staging run: enable probe-first ranking for 10% of traffic on a subset of low-risk routes (no private customers) and compare user p95/p99 and error rates against control.
- Chaos tests: introduce synthetic packet loss between specific POPs and a region to ensure weights shift as expected and rollback works.

Runbook snippets (for on-call)
- If many regions enter TKO at once: check probe fleet health → if healthy, escalate networking (BGP/IXP) and confirm upstream provider status.
- To re-enable an ejected region manually: add region to override allow-list in control plane with a note and temporary ramp policy; monitor for 10 minutes before full reintroduce.
- When control plane is degraded: frontends use last-known ranking and enter conservative mode (prefer local regions if within latency window). Notify customers on affected Dedicated/Private tenants if policy changes would be blocked.

Open questions / TODOs
- How to weight cost (e.g., cross-region egress $) into score for customers on tight budgets? Per-tenant cost sensitivity may require separate score calculus.
- Exact threshold tuning for TKO and ejection windows; need to gather historical incident data to set realistic defaults.
- Interaction with client SDKs: should we expose an API header that explicitly returns the ranked preference list for clients to respect? (pro: better client-side fallbacks; con: opens clients to complexity).

Decision outcome (working hypothesis)
- Move forward with probe-first preference matrix and a centralized control plane that publishes short-lived ranking blobs.
- Implement soft-shift as default failover mode with operator override for immediate failover.
- Anycast frontends use POP-local decisions with consult to control plane; GeoDNS uses short-ttl weighted answers plus overlay where possible.

Next steps (owners assigned)
- Implement scoring service prototype (Maya) — POC 2 weeks.
- Small-scale staging rollout with 10% traffic (Ravi) — coordinate with Observability team for dashboards.
- Add per-tenant cost weight prototype and test on internal customers (Diego).

Notes to self: keep doc concise, capture counterexamples from previous incidents (Nov 2024 cross-Atlantic link flap) and add link to incident timeline in Confluence on next revision.

End of note.
